pos: v. (third person singular of avail: is of force, profits, prevails; rendering Greek ischuo, Hebrew shavah)
etymology: Old French valoir, from Latin valere, to be strong. The Greek James and Paul use is the word for strength: what availeth is what has force.
biblical_def: James: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16). Paul, twice, on what counts in Christ: “in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love” (Gal 5:6); “neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature” (Gal 6:15). Haman, with everything: “Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate” (Est 5:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines avail as to profit; to turn to advantage; to have strength, force, or efficacy sufficient to accomplish the object.
webster_full: AVAIL, v.i. To be of use; to have strength, force or efficacy sufficient to accomplish the object; as, the plea in bar must avail, that is, be sufficient to defeat the suit; this scheme will not avail; medicines will not avail to check the disease.
scriptures: Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
Gal 5:6
For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.
Gal 6:15
For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature.
Est 5:13
Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate.
corruption_summary: Fervency is made the engine of James 5:16, and the verse's condition is a righteous man.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reading of James 5:16 puts the weight on fervent, as if prayer availed in proportion to its heat; the verse puts it on righteous. The Greek says the prayer of a righteous man availeth much, being made effectual — energised — and James's example in the next verse is Elijah, a man of like passions, whose prayer shut heaven because he was a man who stood before the LORD. The force is in the standing, not the feeling. Galatians 5:6 and 6:15 are Paul's two answers to the same question — what availeth in Christ? — and neither answer is a ceremony. Faith which worketh by love; a new creature. Between them they exclude the legalist, whose circumcision availeth nothing, and the antinomian, whose faith does not work. Haman's line is the word's memorial from the other side: all this availeth me nothing, said by a man with everything, over one Jew who would not bow.
roots_summary: Greek ischuo (G2480), to be strong, have force, avail; Hebrew shavah (H7737), to be equal, worth, avail.
roots_lines: Greek ischuo (G2480) — to have force, avail; Galatians 5:6, 6:15, James 5:16.
Hebrew shavah (H7737) — to be worth, avail; Esther 5:13.
usage: “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” — the weight on righteous.
“Neither circumcision availeth any thing… but faith which worketh by love” — the legalist and the antinomian answered together.
“Yet all this availeth me nothing” — Haman with everything.

pos: adj. (fitted, skilled, ready for; in the pastoral epistles, apt to teach; rendering Greek didaktikos, Hebrew phrases for fit for war)
etymology: Latin aptus, fitted, joined. The Greek didaktikos is skilled in teaching — not willing to, but able to, and able in a way that can be examined.
biblical_def: The bishop “must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2). “The servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). Of Asher's sons: “choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes… apt to the war” (1Ch 7:40). Nebuchadnezzar carried away “all that were strong and apt for war” (2Ki 24:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apt as fit, suitable; having a tendency, liable; inclined, disposed; ready, quick; qualified.
webster_full: APT, a. Fit; suitable; as, a story apt to the purpose.
2. Having a tendency; liable; used of things.
3. Inclined; disposed customarily; used of persons.
4. Ready; quick; used of the mental powers; as a pupil apt to learn.
5. Qualified; fit; as, all that were strong and apt for war.
scriptures: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,

All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men.
And all the men of might, even seven thousand, and craftsmen and smiths a thousand, all that were strong and apt for war, even them the king of Babylon brought captive to Babylon.
corruption_summary: Elders are chosen for their success and their sociability, and the one ability Paul required is that they be apt to teach.
corruption_paragraphs: Every qualification for the bishop in 1 Timothy 3 is a character qualification except one, and the one is apt to teach. It is not a willingness or a warmth; the Greek is the skill of a teacher, a competence that can be tested by hearing him, and it is the qualification the church most often waives. Boards are filled with men of business sense, men of standing, men who are liked, and the question whether they can open a passage of Scripture and make it plain is not asked. Paul asked nothing else of the elder's gifts. Second Timothy 2:24 sets the aptness in its company — gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves — because teaching in the church is done to people who resist it, and the apt teacher is the one who can keep teaching when they do.
roots_summary: Greek didaktikos (G1317), skilled in teaching, apt to teach; Hebrew asah milchamah (H6213, H4421), to make war; yatsa tsaba (H3318, H6635), to go out to war.
roots_lines: Greek didaktikos (G1317) — apt to teach; 1 Timothy 3:2, 2 Timothy 2:24 only.
Hebrew osei milchamah (H6213, H4421) — makers of war, apt for war; 2 Kings 24:16; yotse tsaba (H3318, H6635), 1 Chronicles 7:40.
usage: “Apt to teach” — the one gift the elder must have.
“Gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” — teaching people who resist it.
“Strong and apt for war” — the men Nebuchadnezzar took.

pos: n. (in the AV, proof by trial; tried character; rendering Greek dokime, Hebrew nachash and ra'ah)
etymology: Latin experiri, to try, test. Paul's word in Romans 5 is the metal-tester's: what is left after the fire, the proved thing.
biblical_def: Paul's chain: “tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed” (Rom 5:3–5). Laban to Jacob: “I have learned by experience that the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake” (Gen 30:27). The Preacher: “I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge” (Ecc 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines experience as trial, or a series of trials or experiments; observation of a fact or of the same facts and events happening under like circumstances; knowledge derived from trials, use, or practice.
webster_full: EXPERIENCE, n. Trial, or a series of trials or experiments; active effort or attempt to do or to prove something, or repeated efforts.
2. Observation of a fact or of the same facts and events happening under like circumstances.
3. Trial from suffering or enjoyment; suffering itself; the use of the senses.
4. Knowledge derived from trials, use, practice, or from a series of observations.
scriptures: Rom 5:4
And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
And Laban said unto him, I pray thee, if I have found favour in thine eyes, tarry: for I have learned by experience that the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake.
Ecc 1:16

I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.
corruption_summary: Experience is made the authority of religion, and the AV's experience is a proof produced by tribulation, while Laban's was learned by divination.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern believer says my experience of God and means a feeling that settles a question; the Authorized Version's experience is what tribulation leaves behind when patience has done its work — the Greek is the assayer's word, the proved metal — and it produces hope, not authority. Romans 5:4 does not make experience the judge of doctrine; it makes it the evidence that grace has survived a trial. Genesis 30:27 is the warning under the word: Laban learned by experience, and the Hebrew verb is to divine, to read omens. Religion that learns by experience in Laban's sense has become a soothsayer of its own feelings, and it will find, like Laban, that it has been reading the wrong signs. The Preacher had more experience than any man in Jerusalem, and his verdict on it is the next verse: much grief.
roots_summary: Greek dokime (G1382), proof, tried character; Hebrew nachash (H5172), to divine, learn by omens; ra'ah (H7200), to see, experience.
roots_lines: Greek dokime (G1382) — proof, experience; Romans 5:4, 2 Corinthians 2:9, 9:13, Philippians 2:22.
Hebrew nachash, piel (H5172) — to divine, learn by experience; Genesis 30:27, 44:5, 44:15.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, have experience of; Ecclesiastes 1:16.
usage: “Patience, experience; and experience, hope” — the proved metal, not the feeling.
“I have learned by experience” — Laban's verb is to divine.
“My heart had great experience of wisdom” — and the next verse is grief.

pos: v. (to fail to attend to; to disregard; rendering Greek ameleo and parakouo)
etymology: Latin negligere, not to pick up. The Greek of Hebrews 2 is carelessness — not hostility, but not caring — and the verse says it is enough to damn.
biblical_def: “How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him” (Heb 2:3). The Lord on discipline: “if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17). Paul to Timothy: “Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines neglect as to omit by carelessness or design; to forbear to do, use, employ, promote, or attend to; to slight; to treat with inattention.
webster_full: NEGLECT, v.t. To omit by carelessness or design; to forbear to do, use, employ, promote or attend to; as, to neglect duty or business.
2. To omit to receive or embrace; to slight.
3. To slight; not to notice; to forbear to treat with attention or respect.
scriptures: Heb 2:3
How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him;
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
corruption_summary: Men imagine that only rejecting the gospel condemns, and Hebrews asks how they shall escape if they neglect it.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 2:3 is addressed to people who have not rejected anything. They have heard a great salvation, spoken by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard Him, and they have simply not attended to it — let it slip, in the verse before — and the question is how they shall escape. Neglect is the sin of the respectable. It requires no argument against Christ, only a life arranged so that He is never quite the matter at hand, and the writer's point is that a salvation this great cannot be neglected innocently; the size of the thing ignored is the measure of the guilt. Matthew 18:17 gives neglect its church form — the man who neglects to hear the church, twice, is to be treated as an outsider — and 1 Timothy 4:14 its ministerial form: a gift can be neglected until it is gone, and Timothy was told so by name.
roots_summary: Greek ameleo (G272), to be careless of, neglect; parakouo (G3878), to hear amiss, refuse to hear.
roots_lines: Greek ameleo (G272) — to neglect, be careless; Hebrews 2:3, 8:9, 1 Timothy 4:14, Matthew 22:5.
Greek parakouo (G3878) — to neglect to hear, disobey; Matthew 18:17 only.
usage: “How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation” — the sin of the respectable.
“If he neglect to hear the church” — the outsider by his own inattention.
“Neglect not the gift that is in thee” — a gift can be neglected until it is gone.

pos: v. (to turn over, throw down, ruin; rendering Hebrew avvah and haphak)
etymology: Over + turn. Ezekiel's word, said three times over a crown, is ruin; Job's is the turning of the earth by water.
biblical_def: To Zedekiah, the last king of Judah: “Remove the diadem, and take off the crown… I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it: and it shall be no more, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him” (Eze 21:26–27). Job: “he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up: also he sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth” (Job 12:15); He “removeth the mountains, and they know not: which overturneth them in his anger” (Job 9:5); “He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others… he overturneth them in the night” (Job 34:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overturn as to overset; to turn or throw from a basis or foundation; to subvert; to ruin; to destroy; to overpower; to conquer.
webster_full: OVERTURN, v.t. To overset; to turn or throw from a basis or foundation; as, to overturn a carriage or a building.
2. To subvert; to ruin; to destroy; as, to overturn a government.
3. To overpower; to conquer.
scriptures: I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it: and it shall be no more, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him.
Behold, he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up: also he sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth.
Job 9:5
Which removeth the mountains, and they know not: which overturneth them in his anger.
Therefore he knoweth their works, and he overturneth them in the night, so that they are destroyed.
corruption_summary: Thrones are claimed in David's name, and Ezekiel overturned the crown three times until He come whose right it is.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 21:27 is the last word on the throne of David in the Old Testament, and it is a triple overturn. The crown is taken from Zedekiah and the line is not restored — Zerubbabel governs, the Maccabees rule as priests, Herod is an Edomite — and the prophet says the throne shall be no more, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him. That is Shiloh of Genesis 49:10, and the church has always read it of Christ, to whom Gabriel promised the throne of His father David. Every claim to that throne between Zedekiah and Bethlehem was a claim on an overturned crown, and every claim since — the sacral monarchies, the political messiahs, the movements that would seat Christ by force — has forgotten that the giving is God's, and was done. Job's overturnings are the same hand on a larger scale: mountains, waters, and wicked men in the night.
roots_summary: Hebrew avvah (H5754), ruin, overthrow, said three times in Ezekiel 21:27; haphak (H2015), to turn, overturn.
roots_lines: Hebrew avvah avvah avvah (H5754) — ruin, ruin, ruin, overturn, overturn, overturn; Ezekiel 21:27 only.
Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to overturn; Job 9:5, 12:15, 28:9, 34:25.
usage: “I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it… until he come whose right it is” — the crown suspended until Christ.
“He sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth” — the flood in one line.
“He overturneth them in the night” — wicked men, in the open sight of others.

pos: v. (to vomit; rendering Greek emeo, Hebrew qi and qayah)
etymology: Old English spīwan. The Authorized Version keeps the plain word, and gives it to the land in Leviticus and to the Lord in Revelation.
biblical_def: To Laodicea: “So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth” (Rev 3:16). To Israel entering Canaan: “That the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you” (Lev 18:28); “keep all my statutes… that the land, whither I bring you to dwell therein, spue you not out” (Lev 20:22). To the nations, from the cup: “Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall, and rise no more” (Jer 25:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spew as to vomit; to puke; to eject from the stomach; to eject, to cast forth.
webster_full: SPEW, v.t. To vomit; to puke; to eject from the stomach.
2. To eject; to cast forth.
3. To cast out with abhorrence.
scriptures: Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
That the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you.
Ye shall therefore keep all my statutes, and all my judgments, and do them: that the land, whither I bring you to dwell therein, spue you not out.
Therefore thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall, and rise no more, because of the sword which I will send among you.
corruption_summary: The sentimental Christ cannot be sick of anything, and the Lord told a church He would spue it out of His mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 3:16 is the least polite sentence the glorified Christ ever spoke, and He spoke it to a church. He did not say He would rebuke Laodicea, or discipline her, or remove her candlestick; He said He would vomit her, and the plainness is the point — a lukewarm church is not disappointing to Him but nauseating. The Christ of the modern pulpit has no stomach; He accepts, affirms, and accompanies, and is never once revolted. Leviticus 18 gives the older form of the same physiology: the land itself vomited out the Canaanites for their abominations, and Israel is warned that the land has no favourites — defile it, and it will spue you out as it spued them. Creation is not neutral toward abomination. It gags.
roots_summary: Greek emeo (G1692), to vomit; Hebrew qi (H6958) and qayah (H7006), to vomit, spue out.
roots_lines: Greek emeo (G1692) — to vomit, spue; Revelation 3:16 only.
Hebrew qi (H6958) — to vomit out; Leviticus 18:25, 18:28, 20:22, Jonah 2:10; qayah (H7006), Jeremiah 25:27.
usage: “I will spue thee out of my mouth” — a Christ who can be sick of a church.
“That the land spue not you out also” — the land has no favourites.
“Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall” — the cup of the nations.

pos: v. (to hold up, bear, nourish; rendering Hebrew kul and samak)
etymology: Latin sustinere, to hold up from beneath. The Hebrew kul is to contain and so to provide for; the widow who sustained Elijah did it with a barrel.
biblical_def: “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” (Psa 55:22). To Elijah: “get thee to Zarephath… behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee” (1Ki 17:9). Of the wilderness: “forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing; their clothes waxed not old” (Neh 9:21). “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?” (Pro 18:14). David: “I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me” (Psa 3:5). Isaac of Jacob: “with corn and wine have I sustained him” (Gen 27:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sustain as to bear; to uphold; to support; to hold suspended; to keep from sinking in despondence; to maintain, to keep alive.
webster_full: SUSTAIN, v.t. To bear; to uphold; to support; as, a foundation sustains the superstructure.
2. To hold; to keep from falling; as, a rope sustains a weight.
3. To keep from sinking in despondence; to support.
4. To maintain; to keep alive; to support; to subsist; to nourish; as, provisions to sustain a family.
scriptures: Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee.
Neh 9:21
Yea, forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing; their clothes waxed not old, and their feet swelled not.
The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?
Psa 3:5
I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me.
corruption_summary: Psalm 55:22 is read as a promise that the righteous will not be afflicted, and it promises they will not be moved.
corruption_paragraphs: David wrote Psalm 55 betrayed by his friend and fleeing his son, and the verse Peter quotes from it does not promise the removal of either. Cast thy burden upon the LORD — the burden is real and stays a burden — and He shall sustain thee: hold thee up under it. The second clause is the one that gets misquoted: He shall never suffer the righteous to be moved, which is a different thing from never suffering them to be afflicted. The sustained man is still carrying; he is not falling. First Kings 17:9 shows the means God is willing to use: a Gentile widow with a handful of meal, commanded to sustain a prophet, and the prophet sustained by a barrel that did not waste. Providence sustains through instruments that could not sustain themselves, and Nehemiah 9:21 records forty years of it — they lacked nothing — in a place where there was nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew kul, pilpel (H3557), to contain, sustain, provide for; samak (H5564), to uphold, lean upon.
roots_lines: Hebrew kul, pilpel (H3557) — to sustain, nourish; Psalm 55:22, 1 Kings 17:9, Nehemiah 9:21, Genesis 27:37, Proverbs 18:14.
Hebrew samak (H5564) — to uphold, sustain; Psalm 3:5, Isaiah 59:16, Psalm 37:17.
usage: “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee” — held up under it, not relieved of it.
“I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee” — providence through a barrel.
“A wounded spirit who can bear?” — the limit of a man's own sustaining.

pos: adj. (common, profane; without holiness; rendering Hebrew chol, Greek anosios and koinos)
etymology: Un + holy. The Hebrew of Leviticus 10 is the ordinary word for common, and the Greek of Hebrews 10 is the same idea: the blood of the covenant treated as ordinary.
biblical_def: The priest's charge, given the day Nadab and Abihu died: “that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean” (Lev 10:10). The law is made “for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers” (1Ti 1:9); in the last days men shall be “unthankful, unholy, Without natural affection” (2Ti 3:2–3). And the apostate: “who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing” (Heb 10:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unholy as profane, not sacred; not hallowed, not consecrated; impious, wicked.
webster_full: UNHOLY, a. Profane; not sacred; as an unholy place.
2. Not hallowed; not consecrated.
3. Impious; wicked; as unholy men.
scriptures: And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;

Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?

Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
corruption_summary: The church has erased the difference between holy and unholy, and Leviticus 10:10 was the priest's first duty and Hebrews 10:29 the apostate's last sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 10:10 was spoken over two dead priests. Nadab and Abihu had offered strange fire, the fire of the LORD had consumed them, and the charge to their brothers was to put difference between holy and unholy, unclean and clean. Distinguishing is the priestly work, and the modern church has abolished it as a courtesy: the Lord's day is a day, the Lord's table is a snack, the Lord's name is an exclamation, and everything sacred has been made common on the theory that nothing is. Hebrews 10:29 is where the erasure ends. The apostate has counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing — koinos, common, ordinary — and the punishment is sorer than Moses' law, because the thing made common was the only thing that could have made him holy.
roots_summary: Hebrew chol (H2455), common, profane, unholy; Greek anosios (G462), unholy, without piety; koinos (G2839), common, unhallowed.
roots_lines: Hebrew chol (H2455) — common, unholy; Leviticus 10:10, Ezekiel 22:26, 44:23.
Greek anosios (G462) — unholy; 1 Timothy 1:9, 2 Timothy 3:2; koinos (G2839), common, unholy; Hebrews 10:29.
usage: “Put difference between holy and unholy” — the priest's work, given over two dead priests.
“Counted the blood of the covenant… an unholy thing” — the apostate's last sin.
“Unthankful, unholy” — the last days' catalogue.

pos: v. (to make void, cancel, set aside; rendering Greek akuroo and athetesis, Hebrew parar and kaphar)
etymology: Dis + annul, from Latin annullare, to bring to nothing; the prefix strengthens rather than reverses. To disannul is to deprive a thing of its force.
biblical_def: Paul on the covenant: “the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect” (Gal 3:17); “Though it be but a man's covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto” (Gal 3:15). Hebrews: “there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof” (Heb 7:18). God to Job: “Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?” (Job 40:8). Isaiah: “the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it?” (Isa 14:27); and of Judah's bargain, “your covenant with death shall be disannulled” (Isa 28:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disannul as to annul; to make void; to deprive of authority or force; to nullify; to abolish.
webster_full: DISANNUL, v.t. To annul; to make void; to deprive of authority or force; to nullify; to abolish; as, to disannul a law or an ordinance.
scriptures: Gal 3:17
And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect.
Gal 3:15
Brethren, I speak after the manner of men; Though it be but a man's covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto.
Heb 7:18
For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.
Job 40:8
Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?
For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?
And your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it.
corruption_summary: Sinai is made the beginning of God's dealings with His people, and Paul says the covenant of promise came first and the law could not disannul it.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 3:17 is the hinge of covenant theology. The promise to Abraham was a covenant confirmed by God in Christ; the law came four hundred and thirty years later; and a later arrangement cannot disannul an earlier one confirmed — Paul argues it from the way men treat their own contracts. The gospel is therefore older than Sinai. The law was added, for transgressions, till the seed should come, and the covenant of grace runs underneath it the whole way, from the promise to the cross, which is why Abraham was justified by faith and not by a law he never heard. Job 40:8 is disannulling from the other direction: God asks whether Job will make void His judgment to establish his own righteousness, and every self-justification is an attempt to disannul the verdict already given. Isaiah's answer covers both: the LORD hath purposed, and who shall disannul it?

pos: v. (to shake through a sieve, separating grain from chaff; rendering Greek siniazo, Hebrew nua and nuph)
etymology: Old English siftan, from sife, a sieve. The Lord's word to Peter is the only New Testament use, and it is Satan's request.
biblical_def: “And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luk 22:31–32). Amos: “I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth” (Amo 9:9). Isaiah of the LORD's breath: it shall reach to the midst of the neck, “to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity” (Isa 30:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sift as to separate by a sieve, as the fine part of a substance from the coarse; to separate, to part; to examine minutely or critically; to scrutinize.
webster_full: SIFT, v.t. To separate by a sieve, as the fine part of a substance from the coarse; as, to sift meal; to sift powder; to sift sand or lime.
2. To separate; to part.
3. To examine minutely or critically; to scrutinize.
scriptures: And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:
Amo 9:9
For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.

And his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity: and there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err.
corruption_summary: Satan's sifting is imagined as outside God's leave, and the text says he asked for it, and that not the least grain would fall.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 22:31 has a grammar that carries the whole doctrine of perseverance. Satan hath desired to have you — plural, all the disciples — to sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for thee — singular, Peter — that thy faith fail not. The sifting was asked for, as Job's was, and granted; the devil does not sift without leave. And the sifting is a sieve, not a fire: it shakes, it separates the chaff, and Amos 9:9 says what a sieve in God's hand does to the grain — not the least grain falls to the earth. Peter was sifted that night until he cursed and swore, and the chaff of his self-confidence went through the mesh, and the grain was kept, because Someone had prayed. The corruption is to read Peter's fall as evidence that a believer can be lost; the verse reads it as evidence of what the Intercessor's prayer is for. When thou art converted — not if — strengthen thy brethren.
roots_summary: Greek siniazo (G4617), to sift, shake in a sieve; Hebrew nua (H5128), to shake, sift; nuph (H5130), to wave, sift.
roots_lines: Greek siniazo (G4617) — to sift; Luke 22:31 only.
Hebrew nua (H5128) — to shake, sift; Amos 9:9; nuph (H5130), to sift, wave; Isaiah 30:28.
usage: “Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee” — asked for, granted, and prayed over.
“Yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth” — what a sieve in God's hand does to grain.
“To sift the nations with the sieve of vanity” — the LORD's breath.
